text: However, withdrawal is inappropriate in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, despite its good response to treat- ment, as relapse occurs in over 90% of patients • the presence of accompanying neurological or mental deficits.75 Some studies have suggested that mental re- tardation or other neurological deficits are associated with a poorer prognosis on withdrawal; these are proba- bly surrogate markers for symptomatic epilepsy. How- ever, mental retardation is not a contra-indication to withdrawal, and these patients may benefit from the elimination of any sedative effects if other risk factors are absent75 • the age at onset.75,76,83 Several studies have identified a markedly increased risk of relapse on withdrawal in pa- tients with seizure onset in adolescence or adulthood, whereas those with onset before 10 to 12 years of age have a generally more favourable prognosis. This is probably a surrogate marker for particular epileptic syn- dromes or aetiologies • the duration of remission.75,76,83,84 There is evidence in children that waiting for at least 2 seizure-free years be- fore attempting withdrawal is associated with less risk of relapse than doing so earlier. However, the 2-year period was chosen arbitrarily, and the true optimum tim- ing is unknown.84 There is little evidence to guide the timing of withdrawal in adults.84 However, in practice most support a requirement of at least 2 years free from seizures before drug withdrawal75,76,83 • the response to therapy.75 Refractory epilepsy, as indi- cated by the occurrence of seizures once therapy has been begun, or the need for adjunctive or combination therapy to control seizures, is a poor prognostic sign for withdrawal. Patients with a history of multiple seizures before beginning therapy are also at increased risk on withdrawal There is less agreement about the prognostic significance of some other factors: • it is unclear whether the type of drug used to control sei- zures affects the risk of recurrence on withdrawal. It has been suggested that patients taking phenobarbital or benzodiazepines may be at increased risk of relapse, but there is little supportive evidence.75 A poorer prognosis for patients taking valproate has also been reported;85 a study in patients given combination therapy noted an in- creased risk when the carbamazepine component of the regimen was withdrawn.86 It should be borne in mind that withdrawal of an enzyme-inducing antiepileptic may alter the serum concentrations of other drugs in the regimen87 • there is also controversy about the prognostic value of the EEG for the success of withdrawal.75-77,83 Although an abnormal EEG before withdrawal was a negative prognostic factor in many studies, EEG abnormalities are not present in all epileptic patients, and some antie- pileptic drugs suppress EEG abnormalities and can lead to false-negative results75 When a decision
